chapter_text:
CHAPTER 24 - SEMICONDUCTORS AND SEMICONDUCTING DEVICES

Introduction

Modern electronics - computers, mobile phones, televisions, solar panels and countless control systems - rests almost entirely on a single class of materials called semiconductors. A semiconductor is a solid whose ability to conduct electric current lies between that of a good conductor (like copper) and a good insulator (like glass). What makes semiconductors extraordinarily useful is that their conductivity can be controlled precisely - by temperature, by light, and above all by adding tiny, controlled amounts of impurity. This chapter explains why solids behave as conductors, insulators or semiconductors, how we engineer semiconductors by doping, and how junctions of doped material give us diodes and transistors - the building blocks of every electronic circuit.

24.1 ENERGY BANDS IN SOLIDS

In an isolated atom the electrons occupy sharply defined energy levels. When a very large number of atoms (of the order of 10^23) come together to form a solid crystal, the outer electrons of neighbouring atoms interact. The Pauli exclusion principle forbids any two electrons from occupying exactly the same state, so each sharp atomic level splits into an enormous number of very closely spaced levels. Because these levels are so close, they merge into a continuous range of allowed energies called an ENERGY BAND.

Two bands matter most for electrical behaviour:
 - The VALENCE BAND is the band of energies occupied by the outermost (valence) electrons. At absolute zero it is the highest band that is completely or partly filled.
 - The CONDUCTION BAND is the next higher allowed band. Electrons in the conduction band are free to move through the crystal and carry current.

Between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band there may be a range of energies in which no electron states exist. This is the FORBIDDEN ENERGY GAP, of width Eg (measured in electron volts, eV). An electron cannot have an energy that lies within this gap; to move from the valence band into the conduction band it must be given at least Eg of energy.

24.2 CLASSIFICATION OF SOLIDS: CONDUCTORS, INSULATORS AND SEMICONDUCTORS

The size of the forbidden gap, and whether the valence band is full, decides the electrical nature of a solid.

(a) CONDUCTORS (metals): Here the conduction band and valence band overlap, or the valence band is only partly filled. There is effectively no forbidden gap (Eg is nearly zero). Even at ordinary temperatures a huge number of electrons are free to move, so metals conduct very well. Their resistance rises with temperature because lattice vibrations scatter the moving electrons.

(b) INSULATORS: The valence band is completely full and the forbidden gap is large - about 6 eV or more (for diamond Eg is about 6 eV). At room temperature almost no electron has enough thermal energy to jump the gap, so the conduction band stays empty and the material does not conduct.

(c) SEMICONDUCTORS: The forbidden gap is small - about 1 eV (for silicon Eg is about 1.1 eV, for germanium about 0.7 eV). At absolute zero a pure semiconductor is a perfect insulator, because the valence band is full and the conduction band empty. But at room temperature a small number of electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the gap, so the material conducts slightly. As temperature rises, more electrons cross the gap, so - unlike a metal - the conductivity of a semiconductor INCREASES with temperature (its resistance falls).

24.3 INTRINSIC SEMICONDUCTORS

A pure semiconductor, free of any impurity, is called an INTRINSIC semiconductor. Silicon and germanium are the most important; each atom has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours, so at absolute zero every valence electron is locked in a bond and none is free.

When thermal energy breaks a covalent bond, the electron set free jumps to the conduction band, leaving behind a vacancy in the bond. This vacancy behaves like a positive charge carrier and is called a HOLE. Thus thermal excitation always creates carriers in PAIRS - one free electron and one hole - and we speak of ELECTRON-HOLE PAIRS. In an intrinsic semiconductor the number of free electrons (n) exactly equals the number of holes (p): n = p = ni, the intrinsic carrier concentration.

Conduction in a semiconductor is therefore due to TWO kinds of carrier: electrons drifting one way in the conduction band, and holes drifting the opposite way as neighbouring electrons hop into the vacancy. The intrinsic conductivity is small at room temperature and depends strongly on temperature.

24.4 EXTRINSIC SEMICONDUCTORS AND DOPING

Intrinsic semiconductors are too poor as conductors to be useful. Their conductivity is raised enormously, and made controllable, by DOPING - deliberately adding a very small, precise amount of a suitable impurity (typically one impurity atom per million or so). The doped material is called an EXTRINSIC semiconductor. There are two types.

(a) n-TYPE SEMICONDUCTOR: We add a PENTAVALENT impurity - an element with five valence electrons, such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony. Four of its electrons form covalent bonds with the neighbouring silicon atoms; the fifth is loosely bound and, with very little energy, is set free to move in the conduction band. Because each such atom DONATES a free electron, it is called a DONOR. In an n-type semiconductor the free electrons are far more numerous than the holes: electrons are the MAJORITY carriers and holes are the MINORITY carriers. The material as a whole is still electrically neutral.

(b) p-TYPE SEMICONDUCTOR: We add a TRIVALENT impurity - an element with three valence electrons, such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium. Its three electrons form three bonds, but the fourth bond with a neighbouring silicon atom is incomplete - there is a vacancy, that is, a HOLE. Because each such atom can ACCEPT an electron from a neighbouring bond, it is called an ACCEPTOR. In a p-type semiconductor holes are the MAJORITY carriers and electrons the MINORITY carriers. Again the crystal as a whole is neutral.

Doping increases conductivity by several orders of magnitude and lets us decide, at will, whether the majority carriers are negative (n-type) or positive (p-type). This control is the foundation of every semiconductor device.

24.5 THE p-n JUNCTION

If one side of a single semiconductor crystal is doped p-type and the adjacent side n-type, the boundary between them is a p-n JUNCTION. It is the heart of most devices.

At the moment of formation, the n-side has many free electrons and the p-side many holes. Electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side, and holes diffuse from the p-side into the n-side, because of the large concentration difference. As electrons leave the n-side they expose positively charged donor ions there; as holes leave the p-side they expose negatively charged acceptor ions. A narrow region near the junction is thus left with no free carriers, only fixed charged ions - this is the DEPLETION REGION (or depletion layer).

The exposed ions set up an electric field pointing from the n-side to the p-side. This field opposes further diffusion of carriers. The potential difference it represents is the BARRIER POTENTIAL (also called the potential barrier or built-in potential), roughly 0.3 V for germanium and 0.7 V for silicon. Equilibrium is reached when the barrier just stops the net flow of carriers.

24.6 BIASING THE JUNCTION: FORWARD AND REVERSE BIAS

Connecting an external voltage to a p-n junction is called BIASING.

FORWARD BIAS: the p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and the n-side to the negative terminal. The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, so it reduces the barrier and narrows the depletion region. Once the applied voltage exceeds the barrier potential (about 0.7 V for Si), majority carriers cross the junction easily and a large forward current flows. The junction has low resistance in forward bias.

REVERSE BIAS: the p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal. Now the applied voltage adds to the barrier potential, widening the depletion region and raising the barrier. Majority carriers cannot cross. Only a very small REVERSE SATURATION CURRENT flows, carried by the few minority carriers; it is of the order of microamperes and is almost independent of the applied voltage. The junction has very high resistance in reverse bias. If the reverse voltage is raised too far, breakdown occurs.

V-I CHARACTERISTICS OF A JUNCTION DIODE: A device consisting of a single p-n junction with two terminals is a JUNCTION DIODE. Its current-voltage graph shows: in forward bias almost no current until the KNEE (threshold) voltage, after which the current rises steeply; in reverse bias only a tiny, nearly constant reverse current until the breakdown voltage. Because it conducts well one way and blocks the other, a diode acts as a one-way valve for current - the basis of rectification.

24.7 THE DIODE AS A RECTIFIER

Rectification is the process of converting alternating current (a.c.), which reverses direction periodically, into direct current (d.c.), which flows one way. Because a diode conducts only when forward biased, it is the natural rectifier.

HALF-WAVE RECTIFIER: A single diode is placed in series with the a.c. supply and the load. During the half-cycle that forward-biases the diode, current flows through the load; during the other half-cycle the diode is reverse biased and blocks current. The output is a series of one-way pulses - present for one half of each cycle and zero for the other half. It is d.c. (one direction) but very uneven, and half the input is wasted.

FULL-WAVE RECTIFIER: Using either a centre-tapped transformer with two diodes, or four diodes in a BRIDGE arrangement, the circuit delivers current to the load during BOTH half-cycles. In each half-cycle a different diode (or pair of diodes) conducts, but the current through the load is always in the same direction. The output pulses appear twice as often, so full-wave rectified d.c. is much smoother and more efficient than half-wave. A smoothing capacitor (filter) is added to reduce the remaining ripple and give steadier d.c.

24.8 SPECIAL PURPOSE DIODES

(a) ZENER DIODE: A heavily doped junction diode designed to operate safely in reverse breakdown. Beyond its Zener (breakdown) voltage the reverse current rises sharply while the voltage across it stays almost constant. Connected in reverse across a load, it holds the output voltage fixed even when the input voltage or the load current changes - so it works as a VOLTAGE REGULATOR (voltage stabiliser).

(b) LIGHT EMITTING DIODE (LED): A forward-biased junction diode that emits light when electrons and holes recombine across the junction, releasing energy as photons. The colour depends on the semiconductor's energy gap. LEDs are efficient, long-lived and used in indicators, displays and lighting.

(c) PHOTODIODE: A junction diode operated in REVERSE bias and made so that light can fall on the junction. Incident light creates extra electron-hole pairs, increasing the reverse current in proportion to the light intensity. It is used to detect and measure light.

(d) SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic cell): A large-area p-n junction with NO external bias. Sunlight falling on it generates electron-hole pairs; the junction field separates them, producing a voltage and driving a current through an external load. A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy.

24.9 THE JUNCTION TRANSISTOR

A junction transistor is a semiconductor device with TWO p-n junctions formed by three doped regions. It is a three-terminal device used to amplify signals and to switch. There are two types:
 - npn transistor: a thin p-type BASE between two n-type regions (EMITTER and COLLECTOR).
 - pnp transistor: a thin n-type base between two p-type regions.

The three regions are:
 - EMITTER (E): heavily doped; it emits (supplies) the majority carriers.
 - BASE (B): very thin and lightly doped; it controls the flow of carriers.
 - COLLECTOR (C): moderately doped and larger; it collects the carriers.

TRANSISTOR ACTION (npn, normal operation): The emitter-base junction is FORWARD biased and the collector-base junction is REVERSE biased. The forward-biased emitter injects a large number of electrons into the thin base. Because the base is thin and lightly doped, only a very small fraction (about 1 to 5 percent) of these electrons recombine with holes in the base (giving a small base current IB); the great majority (about 95 to 99 percent) are swept across into the reverse-biased collector, forming the collector current IC. By Kirchhoff's current law the emitter current IE = IB + IC. A small base current thus controls a much larger collector current - this is the key to amplification.

24.10 COMMON-EMITTER CONFIGURATION AND CURRENT GAIN

A transistor can be connected in three ways, according to which terminal is common to input and output: common-base, common-emitter and common-collector. The COMMON-EMITTER (CE) configuration - emitter common to both input and output - is the most widely used because it gives high current and power gain.

Two current gain factors are defined:
 - Common-base current gain (alpha): alpha = IC / IE. Because IC is slightly less than IE, alpha is a little less than 1 (typically 0.95 to 0.99).
 - Common-emitter current gain (beta): beta = IC / IB. Because IB is very small, beta is large (typically 20 to 500).

The two are related by:
   beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)   and   alpha = beta / (1 + beta).

Worked example (relating the gains): If alpha = 0.98, then beta = 0.98 / (1 - 0.98) = 0.98 / 0.02 = 49. So a base current is amplified about 49 times at the collector.

Worked example (current gain): In a CE amplifier a base current of 20 microampere produces a collector current of 4 mA. Then beta = IC / IB = 4000 microampere / 20 microampere = 200. The corresponding alpha = beta / (1 + beta) = 200 / 201 = 0.995. The emitter current IE = IB + IC = 20 microampere + 4000 microampere = 4020 microampere = 4.02 mA.

24.11 TRANSISTOR AS AN AMPLIFIER AND AS A SWITCH

AS AN AMPLIFIER: In the CE configuration a small a.c. signal is applied between base and emitter. It causes small changes in the base current, which produce beta times larger changes in the collector current. This collector current flows through a load resistor, and the changing voltage across the load is a magnified (amplified) copy of the input signal. Thus a weak signal is strengthened. The a.c. voltage gain is large, and in CE the output is 180 degrees out of phase with the input.

AS A SWITCH: A transistor can also be operated in just two states. When the base current is zero (or the emitter-base junction is not forward biased), the transistor is in CUTOFF - almost no collector current flows, so it behaves like an OPEN switch. When the base current is large enough, the transistor is driven into SATURATION - maximum collector current flows and the voltage across it is very small, so it behaves like a CLOSED switch. Rapid switching between cutoff and saturation lets transistors act as the ON/OFF elements of digital logic gates and computer memory.

Worked example (rectifier efficiency idea): In a half-wave rectifier fed by a 50 Hz a.c. supply, current flows only during one half of each cycle, so the output pulse appears 50 times a second. In a full-wave rectifier both halves are used, so the output pulses appear 100 times a second - twice as often - which is why full-wave output is smoother.

SUMMARY

- When atoms form a solid, sharp atomic levels broaden into energy bands. The valence band holds the outer electrons; the conduction band, higher up, holds free electrons. Between them may lie a forbidden gap of width Eg.
- Conductors have overlapping or partly filled bands (Eg about 0); insulators have a large gap (about 6 eV or more); semiconductors have a small gap (about 1 eV). Semiconductor conductivity rises with temperature, metal conductivity falls.
- A pure (intrinsic) semiconductor conducts by thermally generated electron-hole pairs, with n = p. Silicon and germanium are tetravalent.
- Doping makes extrinsic semiconductors. Pentavalent donors give n-type material (electrons majority, holes minority); trivalent acceptors give p-type material (holes majority, electrons minority). The crystal stays neutral.
- At a p-n junction, diffusion leaves a depletion region of fixed ions and a barrier potential (about 0.3 V Ge, 0.7 V Si).
- Forward bias lowers the barrier and gives a large current at low resistance; reverse bias raises the barrier and gives only a tiny minority-carrier current at high resistance. A diode is therefore a one-way valve, shown by its V-I characteristic.
- A diode rectifies a.c. into d.c.: half-wave rectifiers use one diode and one half-cycle; full-wave rectifiers use two diodes (centre-tap) or four (bridge) and both half-cycles, giving smoother output.
- Special diodes: the Zener diode regulates voltage in reverse breakdown; the LED emits light on recombination; the photodiode detects light in reverse bias; the solar cell converts light to electricity with no bias.
- A junction transistor (npn or pnp) has emitter, base and collector. With emitter-base forward biased and collector-base reverse biased, a small base current controls a large collector current: IE = IB + IC.
- Current gains: alpha = IC/IE (just under 1), beta = IC/IB (large), with beta = alpha/(1 - alpha). In common-emitter mode the transistor amplifies signals; driven between cutoff and saturation it works as a switch.

chapter_summary.intro: This chapter explains why solids conduct differently using the energy-band picture, how doping turns pure silicon into useful n-type and p-type material, and how p-n junctions build the diode and the transistor - the devices behind all modern electronics.

sections.heading: Energy bands and classification of solids
bullets: In a solid the closely packed atoms make sharp atomic levels split into continuous energy bands; the valence band holds outer electrons and the conduction band holds free electrons.
Between them may lie a forbidden energy gap Eg (in eV) in which no electron states exist.
Conductors have overlapping or partly filled bands (Eg about 0); insulators have Eg about 6 eV or more; semiconductors have Eg about 1 eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV).
Because electrons cross the small gap more easily as temperature rises, a semiconductor's conductivity increases with temperature, while a metal's decreases.

sections.heading: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
bullets: A pure (intrinsic) semiconductor conducts by thermally generated electron-hole pairs, so the electron and hole concentrations are equal (n = p = ni).
Doping adds a tiny controlled impurity to make extrinsic material with much higher, controllable conductivity.
n-type: a pentavalent donor (P, As, Sb) supplies extra free electrons - electrons majority, holes minority.
p-type: a trivalent acceptor (B, Al, Ga, In) creates extra holes - holes majority, electrons minority. Both crystals stay electrically neutral.

sections.heading: The p-n junction diode
bullets: At a p-n junction, carriers diffuse across and leave a depletion region containing only fixed charged ions.
The exposed ions set up a barrier potential (about 0.3 V for Ge, 0.7 V for Si) that stops further diffusion at equilibrium.
Forward bias (p to +, n to -) lowers the barrier and gives a large current at low resistance.
Reverse bias (p to -, n to +) widens the depletion region; only a tiny minority-carrier current flows, so the diode acts as a one-way valve.

sections.heading: Rectifiers and special diodes
bullets: A rectifier converts a.c. to d.c. because a diode conducts in only one direction.
A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes only one half of each cycle; a full-wave rectifier uses two diodes (centre-tap) or four (bridge) and uses both halves, giving smoother output.
A Zener diode works in reverse breakdown at constant voltage and so regulates voltage; an LED emits light when carriers recombine.
A photodiode (reverse biased) detects light; a solar cell (no bias) converts light directly into electricity.

sections.heading: The junction transistor
bullets: A transistor has two junctions and three regions - emitter (heavily doped), base (thin, lightly doped) and collector - as npn or pnp.
In normal operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction reverse biased, so a small base current controls a large collector current: IE = IB + IC.
Current gains: alpha = IC/IE (a little less than 1) and beta = IC/IB (large, 20 to 500), with beta = alpha/(1 - alpha).
In the common-emitter mode the transistor amplifies a signal; switched between cutoff and saturation it acts as an on/off switch for digital circuits.

key_takeaways: The width of the forbidden energy gap Eg decides whether a solid is a conductor (Eg~0), an insulator (~6 eV) or a semiconductor (~1 eV).
Intrinsic semiconductors conduct by electron-hole pairs with n = p; conductivity rises with temperature.
Doping with pentavalent donors gives n-type (electrons majority) and with trivalent acceptors gives p-type (holes majority) material.
A p-n junction has a depletion region and a barrier potential; it conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse bias, acting as a diode.
A diode rectifies a.c. into d.c.; full-wave rectification is smoother than half-wave.
Zener diodes regulate voltage, LEDs emit light, photodiodes detect light and solar cells generate electricity.
In a transistor a small base current controls a large collector current; beta = IC/IB gives amplification, and cutoff/saturation give switching.

The band of energies occupied by the outermost (valence) electrons of the atoms in a solid.
The band of higher energies in which electrons are free to move and carry electric current.
The range of energies between the valence and conduction bands in which no electron states exist; measured in eV.
A pure semiconductor whose conduction is due only to thermally generated electron-hole pairs, so that n = p.
A vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron leaves; it behaves as a mobile positive charge carrier.
Adding a small, controlled amount of impurity to a semiconductor to raise and control its conductivity.
An extrinsic semiconductor doped with a pentavalent donor, in which electrons are the majority carriers.
An extrinsic semiconductor doped with a trivalent acceptor, in which holes are the majority carriers.
The narrow zone near a p-n junction that has no free carriers, only fixed charged donor and acceptor ions.
The built-in potential difference across the depletion region (about 0.3 V for Ge, 0.7 V for Si) that opposes carrier diffusion.
A circuit using diodes that converts alternating current (a.c.) into direct current (d.c.).
A heavily doped diode operated in reverse breakdown at nearly constant voltage, used as a voltage regulator.
A three-terminal semiconductor device with two p-n junctions (npn or pnp) used to amplify signals and to switch.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Semiconductors and Semiconducting Devices
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw circuit and characteristic diagrams where asked. Show all steps in numerical problems and give correct units.

questions.question: Explain, using the energy-band picture, why a semiconductor has a small forbidden gap while an insulator has a large one. Give a typical value of Eg for silicon.
questions.answer: In a solid, atomic levels broaden into a valence band and a higher conduction band separated by a forbidden gap Eg. In a semiconductor this gap is small (for silicon about 1.1 eV), so at room temperature some electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross into the conduction band and the material conducts a little. In an insulator the gap is large (about 6 eV or more, e.g. diamond), so almost no electron can cross it at ordinary temperatures and the material does not conduct.
questions.explanation: Band picture: small gap = semiconductor, large gap = insulator; Si Eg approx 1.1 eV.

questions.question: What is meant by an electron-hole pair? Why does the conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor increase with temperature?
questions.answer: When thermal energy breaks a covalent bond in a pure semiconductor, the freed electron goes to the conduction band and leaves behind a vacancy called a hole; together they form an electron-hole pair, and both carry current. As temperature rises, more bonds break, so more electron-hole pairs are created; with more carriers available the conductivity increases (resistance falls) with temperature.
questions.explanation: Electron-hole pair definition + thermal generation raises carrier number.

questions.question: Distinguish between n-type and p-type semiconductors. Name the impurity used and the majority carrier in each.
questions.answer: n-type: made by doping silicon with a PENTAVALENT impurity (e.g. phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) which donates a free electron; the majority carriers are ELECTRONS and holes are the minority carriers. p-type: made by doping with a TRIVALENT impurity (e.g. boron, aluminium, gallium, indium) which creates a hole; the majority carriers are HOLES and electrons are the minority carriers. Both crystals remain electrically neutral.
questions.explanation: Pentavalent donor -> n-type (electrons); trivalent acceptor -> p-type (holes).

questions.question: What is the depletion region of a p-n junction? What is the barrier potential and its approximate value for silicon and germanium?
questions.answer: When a p-n junction forms, electrons and holes diffuse across and recombine near the boundary, leaving a narrow region containing only fixed charged donor and acceptor ions and no free carriers - this is the depletion region. The fixed ions set up a potential difference across it, the barrier potential, which opposes further diffusion. Its value is about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium.
questions.explanation: Depletion region = fixed ions, no free carriers; barrier ~0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge.

questions.question: Describe the behaviour of a junction diode under forward bias and under reverse bias, and sketch (in words) its V-I characteristics.
questions.answer: Forward bias: the p-side is joined to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal. The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, so the barrier and the depletion region shrink. Once the applied voltage exceeds the knee/threshold voltage (about 0.7 V for Si), majority carriers cross easily and a large forward current flows; the diode has low resistance. Reverse bias: the p-side is joined to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal. The applied voltage adds to the barrier, widening the depletion region, so majority carriers cannot cross. Only a tiny reverse saturation current (microamperes), due to minority carriers, flows and is almost independent of voltage; the diode has very high resistance. V-I characteristic: in the forward region the current is almost zero until the knee voltage, then rises steeply; in the reverse region only a small, nearly constant current flows until the breakdown voltage. Thus the diode conducts one way and blocks the other.
questions.explanation: Forward = low R large current after knee; reverse = high R tiny saturation current; V-I curve shape.

questions.question: With the help of a labelled description, explain the working of a full-wave rectifier and state one advantage over a half-wave rectifier.
questions.answer: A full-wave rectifier delivers current to the load during both halves of each a.c. cycle. In the centre-tapped form, two diodes share a centre-tapped transformer: during one half-cycle the upper diode is forward biased and conducts; during the next half-cycle the lower diode conducts. In the bridge form, four diodes are arranged so that in each half-cycle a different pair conducts. In every half-cycle the current through the load flows in the SAME direction, so the output is d.c. that pulses twice per cycle. Advantage over half-wave: because both halves of the input are used, the output is smoother (higher average d.c., pulses twice as often, less ripple) and the rectifier is more efficient; a filter capacitor then gives steady d.c.
questions.explanation: Both half-cycles used; two/four diodes; output smoother than half-wave.

questions.question: How does a Zener diode act as a voltage regulator? In which bias is it operated?
questions.answer: A Zener diode is operated in REVERSE bias, beyond its Zener (breakdown) voltage. In this region the voltage across the Zener stays almost constant even though the current through it changes a lot. Connected in reverse across the load, it holds the output voltage fixed: if the input voltage or the load current changes, the extra current is taken up by the Zener while the load voltage remains constant. Thus it regulates (stabilises) the voltage.
questions.explanation: Reverse breakdown gives constant voltage -> regulator.

questions.question: In a transistor the emitter current is 5 mA and the base current is 50 microampere. Calculate the collector current, alpha and beta.
questions.answer: IE = IB + IC, so IC = IE - IB = 5 mA - 0.05 mA = 4.95 mA. alpha = IC/IE = 4.95/5 = 0.99. beta = IC/IB = 4.95 mA / 0.05 mA = 4950/50 = 99. (Check: beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) = 0.99/0.01 = 99.)
questions.explanation: IC = IE - IB; alpha = IC/IE; beta = IC/IB.

questions.question: In a common-emitter amplifier a change in base current of 20 microampere causes the collector current to change by 3 mA. Find the current gain beta.
questions.answer: The common-emitter current gain beta = change in IC / change in IB = 3 mA / 20 microampere = 3000 microampere / 20 microampere = 150. So the transistor amplifies the base current 150 times.
questions.explanation: beta = delta IC / delta IB = 3000/20 = 150.

questions.question: State how a transistor works as a switch, naming the two states used.
questions.answer: A transistor used as a switch is operated between two states. In CUTOFF the base current is zero (emitter-base junction not forward biased), so almost no collector current flows and the transistor behaves like an OPEN switch. In SATURATION the base current is large enough that the maximum collector current flows and the voltage across the transistor is very small, so it behaves like a CLOSED switch. Rapid switching between cutoff and saturation makes it the on/off element in digital circuits.
questions.explanation: Cutoff = open (off), saturation = closed (on).

questions.question: Explain how energy bands are formed in a solid.
questions.answer: In an isolated atom, electrons occupy sharp, well-defined energy levels. When about 10^23 atoms come together to form a crystal, the outer electrons of neighbouring atoms interact. The Pauli exclusion principle forbids identical states, so each atomic level splits into a huge number of very closely spaced levels. Because these are so close together, they merge into a practically continuous range of allowed energies called an energy band. The most important are the valence band and the conduction band.
questions.explanation: Many atoms + Pauli principle -> levels split and merge into bands.

questions.question: Classify solids as conductors, insulators and semiconductors on the basis of the forbidden energy gap.
questions.answer: Conductors (metals): valence and conduction bands overlap, so the forbidden gap is nearly zero and many electrons are free; they conduct very well. Insulators: the valence band is full and the forbidden gap is large (about 6 eV or more), so at room temperature almost no electron crosses it and the material does not conduct. Semiconductors: the gap is small (about 1 eV; Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV), so at room temperature a few electrons cross it and the material conducts slightly, with conductivity rising as temperature rises.
questions.explanation: Eg: conductor ~0, insulator ~6 eV, semiconductor ~1 eV.

questions.question: Why does a semiconductor behave as an insulator at absolute zero but conduct at room temperature?
questions.answer: At absolute zero, all valence electrons are locked in covalent bonds; the valence band is completely full and the conduction band empty, so there are no free carriers and the semiconductor behaves as an insulator. At room temperature, thermal energy breaks a few bonds, sending electrons into the conduction band and leaving holes in the valence band. These electron-hole pairs act as carriers, so the material conducts a little.
questions.explanation: 0 K: no free carriers; room temp: thermal pairs conduct.

questions.question: What are majority and minority carriers? Identify them in n-type and p-type semiconductors.
questions.answer: Majority carriers are the more numerous charge carriers in an extrinsic semiconductor; minority carriers are the less numerous ones. In n-type material (pentavalent donor doping) electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers. In p-type material (trivalent acceptor doping) holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers.
questions.explanation: n-type: electrons majority, holes minority; p-type: opposite.

questions.question: How is an n-type semiconductor formed? Why is it electrically neutral?
questions.answer: An n-type semiconductor is formed by doping pure silicon (or germanium) with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony. Four of the impurity's five valence electrons form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms; the fifth is loosely bound and easily becomes a free electron in the conduction band, so electrons are the majority carriers. The crystal is still electrically neutral because each added atom is itself neutral - the extra electron is balanced by the positive charge of its own donor ion nucleus.
questions.explanation: Pentavalent donor gives free electron; neutral overall.

questions.question: How is a p-type semiconductor formed?
questions.answer: A p-type semiconductor is formed by doping pure silicon (or germanium) with a trivalent impurity such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium. The impurity forms only three covalent bonds; the fourth bond is incomplete, leaving a vacancy called a hole. This hole can accept an electron from a neighbouring bond, so the impurity is an acceptor and holes are the majority carriers. The crystal as a whole remains electrically neutral.
questions.explanation: Trivalent acceptor creates holes; holes majority.

questions.question: Explain the formation of the depletion region in a p-n junction.
questions.answer: When a p-n junction is formed, the n-side has many free electrons and the p-side many holes. Because of the concentration difference, electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side into the n-side, where they recombine. This leaves behind fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side near the junction. This narrow region, containing only fixed ions and no free carriers, is the depletion region.
questions.explanation: Diffusion + recombination leaves fixed ions = depletion region.

questions.question: What is the barrier potential and how does it stop further diffusion of carriers?
questions.answer: The fixed positive ions on the n-side and negative ions on the p-side set up an electric field across the depletion region, pointing from the n-side to the p-side. The corresponding potential difference is the barrier potential (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium). This field opposes the diffusion of further majority carriers across the junction; equilibrium is reached when the barrier just balances the tendency to diffuse, so no net current flows.
questions.explanation: Field of fixed ions gives barrier potential opposing diffusion.

questions.question: Describe what happens to a p-n junction diode when it is forward biased.
questions.answer: In forward bias the p-side is connected to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal of the battery. The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, reducing the barrier and narrowing the depletion region. When the applied voltage exceeds the barrier (about 0.7 V for silicon), majority carriers cross the junction easily and a large forward current flows. The diode then offers low resistance.
questions.explanation: Forward bias lowers barrier, large current, low resistance.

questions.question: Describe what happens to a p-n junction diode when it is reverse biased.
questions.answer: In reverse bias the p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal. The applied voltage adds to the barrier potential, widening the depletion region and raising the barrier, so majority carriers cannot cross. Only a very small reverse saturation current (of the order of microamperes), carried by minority carriers, flows, and it is nearly independent of the applied voltage. The diode offers very high resistance.
questions.explanation: Reverse bias raises barrier, tiny minority current, high resistance.

questions.question: Sketch (describe) and explain the V-I characteristics of a junction diode.
questions.answer: In the forward region, the current stays almost zero until the applied voltage reaches the knee (threshold) voltage (about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge); beyond the knee the current rises steeply as voltage increases. In the reverse region, only a tiny, nearly constant reverse saturation current flows, almost independent of voltage, until the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown value, where the current suddenly increases. The curve shows that the diode conducts easily one way and blocks the other.
questions.explanation: Forward: current after knee; reverse: small constant current till breakdown.

questions.question: What is rectification? Why can a diode act as a rectifier?
questions.answer: Rectification is the process of converting alternating current (a.c.), which reverses direction periodically, into direct current (d.c.), which flows only one way. A diode can rectify because it conducts a large current when forward biased but blocks current when reverse biased. So during the half-cycle that forward-biases it, current passes; during the opposite half-cycle it blocks - and the load current is always in one direction.
questions.explanation: Diode conducts one way only, so it converts a.c. to d.c.

questions.question: Explain the working of a half-wave rectifier.
questions.answer: In a half-wave rectifier a single diode is placed in series with the a.c. supply and the load. During the half-cycle that makes the diode forward biased, current flows through the load in one direction. During the next half-cycle the diode is reverse biased and blocks current, so no current flows. The output across the load is therefore a series of one-way pulses, present for one half of each cycle and zero for the other. It is d.c. but very uneven, and half the input power is unused.
questions.explanation: One diode; conducts only one half-cycle; pulsed one-way output.

questions.question: Compare half-wave and full-wave rectification.
questions.answer: A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and lets current pass during only one half of each a.c. cycle, so half the input is wasted and the output is very uneven. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes (centre-tap) or four diodes (bridge) and passes current during both halves of each cycle, always in the same direction through the load. Full-wave output has a higher average d.c. value, pulses twice as often, has less ripple and is more efficient; adding a filter capacitor gives smoother d.c.
questions.explanation: Half-wave: one diode, one half-cycle; full-wave: both halves, smoother.

questions.question: Explain how a Zener diode maintains a constant output voltage.
questions.answer: A Zener diode is connected in reverse across the load and operated beyond its Zener (breakdown) voltage. In this region the voltage across the diode stays almost constant even though the current through it changes greatly. If the input voltage rises or the load current falls, the extra current flows through the Zener while the voltage across it (and hence across the load) stays fixed. In this way it regulates or stabilises the output voltage.
questions.explanation: Constant voltage in reverse breakdown regulates the load.

questions.question: Briefly describe the working and use of an LED and a photodiode.
questions.answer: An LED (light emitting diode) is a forward-biased junction diode; when electrons and holes recombine across the junction, the energy released appears as light (a photon), whose colour depends on the energy gap. LEDs are used as indicators, in displays and for lighting. A photodiode is a junction diode used in reverse bias with light allowed to fall on the junction; incident light creates extra electron-hole pairs, increasing the reverse current in proportion to the light intensity, so it is used to detect and measure light.
questions.explanation: LED: forward, emits light; photodiode: reverse, detects light.

questions.question: How does a solar cell work?
questions.answer: A solar cell is a large-area p-n junction used with no external bias. When sunlight falls on it, the photons create electron-hole pairs near the junction. The built-in electric field of the junction separates them - electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side - producing a potential difference across the cell. If an external load is connected, this drives a current through it. Thus the cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy (photovoltaic effect).
questions.explanation: Light makes pairs; junction field separates them; gives voltage and current.

questions.question: Explain transistor action in an npn transistor.
questions.answer: In an npn transistor the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction reverse biased. The forward-biased emitter injects a large number of electrons into the thin, lightly doped base. Because the base is thin and lightly doped, only a small fraction (about 1 to 5 percent) of these electrons recombine with holes there, giving a small base current IB. The great majority (95 to 99 percent) are swept across the reverse-biased junction into the collector, forming the collector current IC. So IE = IB + IC, and a small base current controls a large collector current.
questions.explanation: Forward EB injects carriers; thin base; most reach collector; IE = IB + IC.

questions.question: Define alpha and beta for a transistor and give the relation between them.
questions.answer: alpha (common-base current gain) is the ratio of collector current to emitter current: alpha = IC/IE. Because IC is slightly less than IE, alpha is a little less than 1 (typically 0.95 to 0.99). beta (common-emitter current gain) is the ratio of collector current to base current: beta = IC/IB, and is large (typically 20 to 500). They are related by beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) and alpha = beta/(1 + beta).
questions.explanation: alpha = IC/IE (<1); beta = IC/IB (large); beta = alpha/(1-alpha).

questions.question: A transistor has alpha = 0.95. Find beta and, if IB = 20 microampere, find IC.
questions.answer: beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) = 0.95/(1 - 0.95) = 0.95/0.05 = 19. Then beta = IC/IB gives IC = beta x IB = 19 x 20 microampere = 380 microampere = 0.38 mA.

questions.question: Explain how a transistor works as an amplifier in the common-emitter configuration.
questions.answer: In the common-emitter amplifier a small a.c. signal is applied between base and emitter, on top of the d.c. forward bias. It causes small changes in the base current IB. Because the collector current IC = beta x IB, these produce beta times larger changes in the collector current. The collector current flows through a load resistor, and the changing voltage across this resistor is a magnified (amplified) copy of the input signal. Thus a weak input signal is strengthened; in CE the output is 180 degrees out of phase with the input.
questions.explanation: Small IB change -> beta times larger IC change -> amplified output across load.

questions.question: Explain how a transistor is used as a switch.
questions.answer: A transistor used as a switch is driven between two extreme states. When the base current is zero (or the emitter-base junction is not forward biased), the transistor is in cutoff: almost no collector current flows, so between collector and emitter it behaves like an open switch (OFF). When the base current is made large enough, the transistor enters saturation: the maximum collector current flows and the collector-emitter voltage is very small, so it behaves like a closed switch (ON). Rapidly switching between cutoff and saturation makes the transistor the on/off element of digital circuits.
questions.explanation: Cutoff = OFF (open), saturation = ON (closed).

questions.question: Explain, with the help of the energy-band model, how conductors, insulators and semiconductors differ. Include typical values of the forbidden energy gap.
questions.answer: In a solid, the sharp atomic energy levels broaden into energy bands. The valence band contains the outer electrons; the conduction band (higher energy) contains electrons that are free to move and carry current. Between them may lie a forbidden energy gap Eg in which no electron states exist. (1) Conductors (metals): the conduction and valence bands overlap, or the valence band is only partly filled, so Eg is nearly zero. Many electrons are free even at ordinary temperature, giving high conductivity; resistance rises with temperature because of increased scattering. (2) Insulators: the valence band is completely full and Eg is large (about 6 eV or more, e.g. diamond). At room temperature almost no electron can jump the gap, so the conduction band stays empty and the material does not conduct. (3) Semiconductors: Eg is small (about 1 eV; silicon 1.1 eV, germanium 0.7 eV). At 0 K they are insulators, but at room temperature a few electrons cross the gap, forming electron-hole pairs and giving slight conduction. As temperature rises, more pairs form, so a semiconductor's conductivity increases with temperature - the opposite of a metal.
questions.explanation: Band model + Eg values distinguish the three classes and their temperature behaviour.

questions.question: Explain intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors. Describe how n-type and p-type materials are produced and identify their majority and minority carriers.
questions.answer: An intrinsic semiconductor is a chemically pure semiconductor such as pure silicon or germanium. Each atom is tetravalent and forms four covalent bonds. At room temperature thermal energy breaks a few bonds, creating electron-hole pairs; the free electron goes to the conduction band and the hole stays in the valence band. In intrinsic material the electron and hole concentrations are equal (n = p), and the conductivity is small. Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping - adding a tiny controlled amount of impurity - which raises conductivity greatly and lets us choose the majority carrier. (a) n-type: doping with a pentavalent donor (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony). Four of the five valence electrons bond; the fifth becomes a free electron. Electrons are the majority carriers, holes the minority carriers. (b) p-type: doping with a trivalent acceptor (boron, aluminium, gallium, indium). Only three bonds form; the missing fourth bond is a hole. Holes are the majority carriers, electrons the minority carriers. In both cases the crystal remains electrically neutral because the added atoms are themselves neutral.
questions.explanation: Intrinsic n=p; doping gives n-type (electrons) and p-type (holes); crystals neutral.

questions.question: Describe the formation of a p-n junction and explain, with the help of biasing, why a diode conducts in one direction only.
questions.answer: A p-n junction is formed within a single crystal, one side doped p-type and the adjacent side n-type. At formation, electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side diffuse across and recombine, leaving fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side. This carrier-free region of fixed ions is the depletion region, and the ions set up a barrier potential (about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge) that opposes further diffusion. Forward bias (p to +, n to -): the applied voltage opposes the barrier, narrowing the depletion region; once it exceeds the barrier, majority carriers cross freely and a large forward current flows (low resistance). Reverse bias (p to -, n to +): the applied voltage adds to the barrier, widening the depletion region so majority carriers cannot cross; only a tiny minority-carrier reverse saturation current flows (high resistance). Because it conducts strongly in forward bias but blocks in reverse bias, a junction diode is a one-way device - it conducts in only one direction.
questions.explanation: Depletion region + barrier; forward conducts, reverse blocks -> one-way diode.

questions.question: Explain the working of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers and compare their outputs.
questions.answer: A rectifier uses diodes to convert a.c. into d.c. because a diode conducts only when forward biased. Half-wave rectifier: a single diode is in series with the a.c. supply and the load. During the half-cycle that forward-biases the diode, current flows through the load; during the other half-cycle the diode is reverse biased and blocks current. The output is one-way pulses present for only half of each cycle - uneven d.c., with half the input unused. Full-wave rectifier: using a centre-tapped transformer with two diodes, or four diodes in a bridge, the circuit passes current to the load during both half-cycles. In each half-cycle a different diode (or pair) conducts, but the load current is always in the same direction, so the output pulses appear twice per cycle. Comparison: full-wave output has a higher average d.c. value, twice the pulse frequency, less ripple and better efficiency than half-wave. A filter capacitor is usually added to smooth the pulsating d.c. into steadier d.c.
questions.explanation: Half-wave one diode/one half-cycle; full-wave both halves; full-wave smoother.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of the four special-purpose diodes: Zener diode, LED, photodiode and solar cell.
questions.answer: (1) Zener diode: a heavily doped p-n junction designed to work safely in reverse breakdown. Beyond its Zener voltage, the reverse current rises sharply while the voltage across it stays nearly constant. Connected in reverse across a load, it holds the output voltage fixed against changes in input voltage or load current, so it is used as a voltage regulator. (2) LED (light emitting diode): a forward-biased junction diode in which electrons and holes recombine at the junction and release energy as light; the colour depends on the energy gap. It is used in indicators, displays and lighting because it is efficient and long-lived. (3) Photodiode: a junction diode operated in reverse bias with light allowed to reach the junction; incident light creates extra electron-hole pairs, increasing the reverse current in proportion to the light intensity, so it detects and measures light. (4) Solar cell: a large-area p-n junction used with no external bias; sunlight generates electron-hole pairs which the junction field separates, producing a voltage that drives current through an external load, converting light directly into electricity.
questions.explanation: Zener regulates; LED emits; photodiode detects; solar cell generates.

questions.question: With a labelled description, explain the construction of an npn transistor and its action in the common-emitter configuration.
questions.answer: An npn transistor has three doped regions forming two junctions: a heavily doped emitter (n), a very thin and lightly doped base (p), and a moderately doped, larger collector (n). In normal operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction reverse biased. The forward-biased emitter injects a large number of electrons into the thin base. Because the base is thin and lightly doped, only about 1 to 5 percent of these electrons recombine with holes there (small base current IB); the remaining 95 to 99 percent are swept by the reverse-biased collector junction into the collector (collector current IC). Thus IE = IB + IC, and a small base current controls a much larger collector current. In the common-emitter configuration the emitter is common to input and output; the input (a.c. signal) is applied between base and emitter and the output is taken between collector and emitter. Because IC = beta x IB with beta large, small changes in base current cause large changes in collector current, giving high current and power gain - the basis of amplification.
questions.explanation: npn regions/biasing; thin base; IE=IB+IC; CE gives large gain.

questions.question: Explain how a junction transistor can be used both as an amplifier and as a switch.
questions.answer: As an amplifier (common-emitter): the transistor is biased so the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction reverse biased. A small a.c. signal applied between base and emitter causes small variations in the base current IB. Since the collector current IC = beta x IB and beta is large, IC varies beta times as much. This varying collector current flows through a load resistor, and the varying voltage across it is an amplified copy of the input signal (180 degrees out of phase in CE). As a switch: the transistor is driven between two states. In cutoff (base current zero) almost no collector current flows, so it behaves like an open switch (OFF). In saturation (large base current) maximum collector current flows and the collector-emitter voltage is very small, so it behaves like a closed switch (ON). Fast switching between cutoff and saturation makes the transistor the on/off element in logic gates and computer memories.
questions.explanation: Amplifier: small IB -> large IC change across load; switch: cutoff (off)/saturation (on).

questions.question: Explain why the conductivity of a pure semiconductor increases with temperature, whereas that of a metal decreases. Relate your answer to the energy-band picture.
questions.answer: In a pure semiconductor there is a small forbidden gap (about 1 eV). At low temperature almost all valence electrons are bound, so few carriers exist and conductivity is low. As temperature rises, more thermal energy is available, so more covalent bonds break and more electrons cross from the valence band into the conduction band, each leaving a hole. The number of electron-hole pairs grows rapidly with temperature; with many more carriers, the conductivity increases (resistance falls). In a metal the conduction and valence bands overlap, so the number of free electrons is already very large and hardly changes with temperature. However, as temperature rises the lattice ions vibrate more strongly and scatter the moving electrons more often, reducing their drift and so increasing resistance. Hence a metal's conductivity decreases with temperature. The opposite temperature behaviour of the two materials thus follows directly from the band picture: carrier NUMBER controls the semiconductor, while carrier SCATTERING controls the metal.
questions.explanation: Semiconductor: more pairs with T; metal: more scattering with T.

questions.question: A teacher draws the band diagrams of three solids A, B and C. In A the valence and conduction bands overlap. In B they are separated by a gap of about 1 eV. In C they are separated by a gap of about 6 eV. (a) Classify A, B and C. (b) Which of them is silicon likely to resemble? (c) What happens to the conductivity of B as temperature rises? (d) Why does A conduct even at 0 K?
questions.answer: (a) A is a conductor (overlapping bands, Eg ~ 0); B is a semiconductor (small gap ~1 eV); C is an insulator (large gap ~6 eV). (b) Silicon (Eg ~ 1.1 eV) resembles B, a semiconductor. (c) As temperature rises, more electron-hole pairs are created in B, so its conductivity increases (resistance falls). (d) A conducts even at 0 K because its bands overlap, so free electrons are always available with no gap to cross.
questions.explanation: Identify classes by Eg; Si is a semiconductor; semiconductor conductivity rises with T; metal always conducts.

questions.question: A student takes pure silicon and dops one sample with phosphorus and another with boron. (a) Which sample is n-type and which is p-type? (b) Name the majority carrier in each. (c) Is either sample electrically charged overall? (d) Which impurity is a donor and which an acceptor?
questions.answer: (a) The phosphorus-doped sample is n-type (phosphorus is pentavalent); the boron-doped sample is p-type (boron is trivalent). (b) In the n-type sample electrons are the majority carriers; in the p-type sample holes are the majority carriers. (c) Neither sample is charged overall - both remain electrically neutral because the added atoms are themselves neutral. (d) Phosphorus is a donor (donates a free electron); boron is an acceptor (accepts an electron, creating a hole).
questions.explanation: Pentavalent P -> n-type/donor; trivalent B -> p-type/acceptor; both neutral.

questions.question: A silicon p-n junction diode is connected in a circuit. First the p-side is joined to the + terminal of a battery, then the connections are reversed. (a) Name the two biasing conditions. (b) In which case does a large current flow? (c) What is the approximate voltage that must be exceeded for conduction? (d) What kind of current flows in the other case and who carries it?
questions.answer: (a) When the p-side is joined to the + terminal it is forward biased; after reversing, it is reverse biased. (b) A large current flows in forward bias. (c) The applied voltage must exceed the barrier (knee) voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon. (d) In reverse bias only a very small reverse saturation current (of the order of microamperes) flows, carried by the minority carriers.
questions.explanation: Forward vs reverse bias; forward conducts above ~0.7 V; reverse = tiny minority current.

questions.question: In a laboratory, an a.c. voltage is applied to (i) a single diode with a load, and (ii) a bridge circuit of four diodes with a load. (a) Name each type of rectifier. (b) In which one does the load receive current during both half-cycles? (c) Which output has less ripple? (d) What extra component is added to make the output smoother?
questions.answer: (a) Circuit (i) is a half-wave rectifier and circuit (ii) is a full-wave (bridge) rectifier. (b) The bridge (full-wave) circuit delivers current to the load during both half-cycles. (c) The full-wave (bridge) output has less ripple. (d) A filter (smoothing) capacitor is added across the load to reduce ripple and make the d.c. output smoother.
questions.explanation: One diode = half-wave; four = full-wave bridge; full-wave both halves, smoother; add capacitor.

questions.question: A power supply must give a steady 5 V d.c. even though the input voltage fluctuates. An engineer connects a Zener diode of Zener voltage 5 V in reverse across the load. (a) In which bias is the Zener operated? (b) What stays almost constant across it in this region? (c) What function does the Zener perform here? (d) What happens to the extra current when the input voltage rises?
questions.answer: (a) The Zener diode is operated in reverse bias, beyond its breakdown (Zener) voltage. (b) The voltage across it stays almost constant (about 5 V) even though the current changes. (c) It acts as a voltage regulator (stabiliser), keeping the output voltage steady. (d) When the input voltage rises, the extra current flows through the Zener diode while the voltage across it (and the load) stays fixed at about 5 V.
questions.explanation: Zener reverse breakdown gives constant voltage = regulator.

questions.question: Two students discuss light-based diodes. One holds an LED, the other a photodiode. (a) Which one gives out light and in which bias? (b) Which one detects light and in which bias? (c) What determines the colour of the LED's light? (d) How does light change the current in the photodiode?
questions.answer: (a) The LED gives out light and is operated in forward bias; light is produced when electrons and holes recombine at the junction. (b) The photodiode detects light and is operated in reverse bias. (c) The colour of the LED's light is determined by the energy gap of the semiconductor used. (d) Light falling on the photodiode creates extra electron-hole pairs, so the reverse current increases in proportion to the light intensity.
questions.explanation: LED forward emits; photodiode reverse detects; colour from Eg; light raises reverse current.

questions.question: In a transistor circuit, the emitter current is measured as 10 mA and the base current as 100 microampere. (a) Find the collector current. (b) Calculate alpha. (c) Calculate beta. (d) State which current is the smallest and why.
questions.answer: (a) IC = IE - IB = 10 mA - 0.1 mA = 9.9 mA. (b) alpha = IC/IE = 9.9/10 = 0.99. (c) beta = IC/IB = 9.9 mA / 0.1 mA = 99. (d) The base current (100 microampere) is the smallest, because the base is thin and lightly doped, so only a small fraction of the injected carriers recombine there while most pass on to the collector.
questions.explanation: IC=IE-IB=9.9 mA; alpha=0.99; beta=99; base current smallest.

questions.question: A transistor is used first to strengthen a weak microphone signal and later as an on/off switch in a digital circuit. (a) Which configuration is commonly used for amplification? (b) What controls the large collector current in amplification? (c) Name the two states used when it acts as a switch. (d) In which switching state does maximum collector current flow?
questions.answer: (a) The common-emitter (CE) configuration is commonly used for amplification. (b) A small base current controls the large collector current (IC = beta x IB), so the small input signal controls a much larger output. (c) The two states used as a switch are cutoff (OFF) and saturation (ON). (d) Maximum collector current flows in the saturation state (the ON, closed-switch state).
questions.explanation: CE amplifier; base current controls IC; switch uses cutoff/saturation; saturation = max IC.

questions.question: A pure germanium crystal is cooled to nearly absolute zero and then warmed to room temperature. (a) How does it behave electrically at 0 K? (b) What carriers appear as it warms? (c) How does its conductivity change with rising temperature? (d) How does this behaviour differ from that of a copper wire?
questions.answer: (a) At nearly 0 K the pure germanium behaves as an insulator, because all valence electrons are bound and the conduction band is empty. (b) As it warms, thermal energy breaks bonds, creating electron-hole pairs; both electrons and holes act as carriers. (c) Its conductivity increases (resistance falls) as temperature rises, because more electron-hole pairs are created. (d) A copper wire behaves oppositely: its conductivity decreases (resistance rises) with temperature, because increased lattice vibration scatters its already-plentiful free electrons.
questions.explanation: Ge: insulator at 0 K, conductivity rises with T; copper opposite.

questions.question: A common-emitter amplifier has a transistor with beta = 100. The input base current changes by 30 microampere due to a signal. (a) Find the change in collector current. (b) If the base current were instead controlled to fall to zero, what state is the transistor in? (c) What is this state called in switching? (d) State one everyday use of a transistor switch.
questions.answer: (a) Change in IC = beta x change in IB = 100 x 30 microampere = 3000 microampere = 3 mA. (b) With zero base current almost no collector current flows, so the transistor is effectively off (behaving like an open switch). (c) This state is called cutoff. (d) A transistor switch is used in digital logic gates and computer memory (or to switch devices such as LEDs, relays or motors on and off).
questions.explanation: delta IC = 100 x 30 uA = 3 mA; zero IB = cutoff (off); used in digital circuits.
